AI for Eyes

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How 21st century tech is assisting the blind and visually impaired

Unique Selling Point:
Low tech solutions like white canes, guide dogs and Braille have been around for decades or even centuries to help make life a little easier for those who cannot see. But a new wave of smart technology, machine learning and virtual reality devices is changing the way the visually impaired are accessing the world around them.

Summary:
Apps and smart devices have begun to dominate the way we interact with the world around us - and it's no different for people living with a visual impairment. From brand new (and pricey) wearable VR devices to smart refreshable braille (replacing 50s style braille typewriters) and even free apps, the world of assistive tech is expanding at a rapid pace - and perhaps even helping the blind to achieve a greater level of independence than ever before.

We will look first at wearable devices, which have leveraged off the VR and MR technology released by Google and Microsoft in recent years. Although wearable VR did not take off as much as anticipated in the mainstream, it's had a big impact on assistive tech. We'll speak to two or three people who use different wearable devices about the impact they have had on their lives.

We will also meet Mukthar Khan, who works for assistive tech company Sensory Solutions. He is blind himself and can talk about the challenges of being blind especially in SA, as well as the various devices developed to help. He will show us the refreshable braille device which allows import of text documents, note taking and interface with a phone - on one deceptively simple, small black box. He will also talk to us about the various apps that are available, often free of charge.

Further information:
1. WEARABLE DEVICES
eSight is a wearable device that augments the vision of low-vision (or legally blind) people by filming the world in real time, projecting it onto screens in front of the user's eyes, and then magnifying and enhancing the images according to the user's needs. We'll speak to 17 year old Marle van Wyk, who says her life has been changed by eSight, and Johan Grove, who can show us how a user is assessed and fitted.
NuEyes is another wearable device which was developed for use in the military. It operates in a very similar way to eSight but comes in at less than half the price, for $4500.

2. APPS
Seeing AI is an app that uses image recognition and machine learning to recognise and describe faces, scenes and objects, and can read text on documents or street signs. It's developed by Microsoft and available for free.
BeSpecular is a locally developed app that calls on crowd sourced volunteering. Both blind users and sighted volunteers download the app and sign up. Then when a blind person needs help with a task that requires sight (like picking a colour of shirt, reading a temperature gauge or a food label etc) they use the app to take a picture and record a voice message of their request. The request is sent to a number of sighted volunteers who can respond, listen to the message and type or record a response. This is a local version of other apps that are available around the world (another one is called Be My Eyes) and hopefully we will speak to the developer.

Extra Budget Items:
Interviews in Cape Town - one case study and an expert.

Press Release:


Low tech solutions like white canes, guide dogs and Braille have been around for decades or even centuries to help make life a little easier for those who cannot see. But a new wave of smart technology, machine learning and virtual reality devices is changing the way the visually impaired are accessing the world around them.

Script:


UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: At 8 years old I started seeing badly. I started to stand up and walk towards the board and put like my nose on the board and then went back and then write down the answer and then I realised that is not normal.
LINK1: Over 250 million people are estimated to be living with a visual impairment worldwide – the majority in developing countries. Most of us will lose at least part of our vision as we age. For some, the devastation starts early.
VO1: Marlé van Wyk has less than 10% vision, thanks to Stargardt’s Disease, a form of macular degeneration that destroys the detailed central vision responsible for recognising faces or reading.
UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: When my hand is like this, I can’t see my hand. It looks like my hand is cut off. But when it’s bringing it closer, it just looks like there is a hole in the middle of my hand.
VO2: Visual impairment can be caused by anything from a hereditary condition, to brain trauma. In South Africa, most visually impaired people live in disadvantaged areas. Only 3% are employed, says Occupational Therapist and assistive technology advisor Zoe Michaelides.
UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: That means that there is a vast majority of people who are living with visual impairment or are legally blind who are actually not participating fully in society and not contributing. So one would expect that they are feeling large degrees of isolation and occupational deprivation.
UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: My dream is to drive a car and I’m not allowed to drive a car. And it’s hard for me to see how all of my friends can start driving and be capable of doing things that I can’t do.
LINK2: Do you wear glasses? Or contact lenses? Then this is a familiar setting for you – and so is that feeling of disorientation when your vision is blurred. Now imagine you couldn’t correct that with a simple prescription.
VO3: Instead, many visually impaired people rely on bulky assistive devices or help from friends and family to do basic daily tasks. But technology is opening up a whole new world.
UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: eSight augments reality. So you’re able to magnify into your world.
VO4: No, it’s not a Sci-fi movie. eSight is a wearable device that enhances the little vision Marlé has. A camera streams a live image to screens in front of her eyes, where she can manipulate it with a handheld control.
UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: Control the contrast, control the colour, control the brightness in a way that their eyes might not be able to do for them.
VO5: Now instead of pressing her nose to the blackboard, Marlé can digitally zoom in close enough to bypass her blind spot. She can freeze frame, change colours so text is easier to read, and stream video directly to her eyes. eSight can even read text aloud.
UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: I looked out of the window and I saw on the water of the sea the little waves it made. The ocean just looks flat for me. And for the first time I could see that it’s wobbly and not flat.
UPSOUND: Johan Grové: We have three grandchildren, little girls all of them. And it’s amazing for me because I can really see the detail on their faces, which wouldn’t be possible for me without this pair of glasses.
VO6: Johan Grové was diagnosed with Stardgardt’s Disease at 15. As a Specific Needs consultant for Vodacom, he tests devices and programmes for accessibility.
UPSOUND: Johan Grové: Having worked with assistive devices of all sorts and all sizes over 26 years, I have never come across a product like this that can do so many things in one device. I can even go on a game drive. There was giraffes about 100, 150m away on our right hand side. Normally I wouldn’t even bother looking because I just can’t see that far. And I could zoom in to a point where I could see the skin of the giraffe.
VO7: Assistive tech was not what many of us had in mind when we were introduced to augmented reality. In fact, it was developed for completely different uses, from gaming to warfare.
UPSOUND: Nicholas Rose: Being a military specification item, it’s robust and of course it’s real cool too. It projects a stereoscopic image of 65 inches like looking at a big TV set hovering in front of you.
VO8: Sir Nicholas Rose discovered NuEyes after corneal ulcers demolished the vision in his left eye, and left his right cornea so scarred he sees as if through a misted window. Unable to recognise his patients, he was forced to end his 40-year career as an optometrist.
UPSOUND: Nicholas Rose: I show-jumped international show-jumping, I played international polo on horseback, I did medieval armoured combat, I flew helicopters, I rode motorbikes, I did water skiing, yacht racing. Your life goes from 1000km/h to zero.
VO9: NuEyes enhances a live image using this tiny remote, on-board controls, or voice commands.
UPSOUND: Devi Sankaree Govender: Glasses make bigger. That’s like Harry Potter stuff!
Well I can tell you even our camera crew look better with it on. Well done guys.
Nicholas Rose: Now without the NuEyes I can’t even see this E. With the NuEyes I can get down to this 20/20 vision.
Devi Sankaree Govender: I could do with a pair for spyware in my line of work.
VO10: Nicholas has even begun work again as a low-vision optometrist distributing NuEyes.
UPSOUND: Devi Sankaree Govender: How has this changed your life?
Nicholas Rose: I can watch a polo game without holding up a pair of binoculars. I can watch polo. I can watch show jumping. And see it very clearly. I can go into a supermarket and see what we’re actually buying and what the prices are and that.
UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: It’s sometimes the little things. So it allows them engagement in simple activities of daily living that some of us might take for granted.
VO11: But few can afford the hefty dollar price tag. And these wearable devices only augment low vision: they’re useless to the totally blind.
But another revolutionary assistive device is probably sitting in your pocket right now.
LINK3: These days, we barely move without consulting an app. For most of us, a smart phone represents convenience, but for the visually impaired this little device is a lifeline.
VO12: Many standard smart phones are now blind accessible and hundreds of apps offer assistance at an affordable price or even for free. They can identify colour, describe objects, recognise faces, and even narrate the world around you.
UPSOUND: Johan Grové: In the past I had to run to the wine cooler, take out the bottle, come back to my wife, she’s busy preparing food. What is this, ok that’s not what I want, and you go back. So now it’s much easier.
LINK4: Shopping for groceries – it’s such an everyday job. But try telling cinnamon from chilli when you can’t see the labels.
UPSOUND: Johan Grové: That’s a Spier from the Spier landgoed. That’s good, we can take that one.
VO13: Now Johan doesn’t have to see the label – he can use a QR and barcode scanner to identify the product he wants.
UPSOUND: [app reads product name: House of Coffees]
Johan Grové: House of Coffees Italian blend 250g. That’s exactly what I want.
UPSOUND: Devi Sankaree Govender: What have the latest developments meant personally for you?
Johan Grové: One word, independence. It gives you back your independence. It gives you the ability to take your phone, call a car, get in the car and drive somewhere. It gives me independence to read whatever I want to read wherever I am.
UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: Machine learning is doing enormous progress in looking at the pictures and so on, but we still have a long way to go before you can really trust an algorithm to do this.
VO14: Loss of his peripheral vision and years working with the blind inspired Hans Jørgen Wiberg to create Be My Eyes, a free app that connects a visually impaired person to a sighted volunteer via live video.
UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: I like to call it micro-volunteering. We have quite a few calls that are like 20 seconds: Have I set my oven to 200 degrees? Yes you have. Oh, thank you very much. And so it’s a super super convenient way to be a volunteer.
VO15: The app has 100 000 visually impaired users. 1.7 million volunteers have signed up to lend their eyes to the blind, who can now get 24/7 help from any time-zone, in 183 languages.
UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: We even have had a blind girl who made a pregnancy test. And she was using Be My Eyes to have the result of this pregnancy test read to her. It’s really her only way to get this super personal information at her own terms.
VO16: So while it remains to be seen what medical advances will do for the visually impaired, independence is cheaper and more available today than ever before.
UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: Every time you have a friend over, then you have a long list of can you please do this and this and this. And now you can just drink coffee with your friends.
UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: Ten years ago when I was diagnosed with the disease, there was nothing that could help me see better. It has given me opportunities that I’ve never had before.
UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: If ever there was a time to be working with a preferred ability or different ability, it would be this time because people are able to compete on the same playing field in the digital world.

PROMOS

PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS
VO: Over 250 million people worldwide live with impaired vision. It’s an age-old problem – but machine learning and augmented reality are offering new solutions.

PROMO 2: 15 SECONDS
VO: Assistive tech may not be the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the words “augmented reality”. But it’s opening up new worlds for the visually impaired.
UPSOUND: [10:43:32][…] Nicholas: with the NuEyes I can get down to this 20/20 vision.
Devi: I could do with a pair for spyware.

PROMO 3: 15 SECONDS
UPSOUND: [app reads product name: House of Coffees]
Johan: House of Coffees Italian blend. That’s exactly what I want.
VO: From high-end wearable devices to free apps, independence for the visually impaired is more available today than ever before.
UPSOUND: Marle [10:14] […] it has given me opportunities that I’ve never had before.

PROMO 4: 30 SECONDS
UPSOUND: Marle [01:18] […] I can’t see my hand. It looks like my hand is cut off. But when it’s bringing it closer, it just looks like there is a hole in the middle of my hand.
VO: Marle van Wyk is one of over 250 million people worldwide living with a visual impairment. But the age of augmented reality offers some cutting edge assistive solutions.
UPSOUND: Zoe [08:23] if ever there was a time to be working with a preferred ability or different ability, it would be this time

Carte Blanche HD Nikola Vrahimis 07 January 2019 Press Release: Low tech solutions like white canes, guide dogs and Braille have been around for decades or even centuries to help make life a little easier for those who cannot see. But a new wave of smart technology, machine learning and virtual reality devices is changing the way the visually impaired are accessing the world around them. Script: UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: At 8 years old I started seeing badly. I started to stand up and walk towards the board and put like my nose on the board and then went back and then write down the answer and then I realised that is not normal. LINK1: Over 250 million people are estimated to be living with a visual impairment worldwide – the majority in developing countries. Most of us will lose at least part of our vision as we age. For some, the devastation starts early. VO1: Marlé van Wyk has less than 10% vision, thanks to Stargardt’s Disease, a form of macular degeneration that destroys the detailed central vision responsible for recognising faces or reading. UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: When my hand is like this, I can’t see my hand. It looks like my hand is cut off. But when it’s bringing it closer, it just looks like there is a hole in the middle of my hand. VO2: Visual impairment can be caused by anything from a hereditary condition, to brain trauma. In South Africa, most visually impaired people live in disadvantaged areas. Only 3% are employed, says Occupational Therapist and assistive technology advisor Zoe Michaelides. UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: That means that there is a vast majority of people who are living with visual impairment or are legally blind who are actually not participating fully in society and not contributing. So one would expect that they are feeling large degrees of isolation and occupational deprivation. UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: My dream is to drive a car and I’m not allowed to drive a car. And it’s hard for me to see how all of my friends can start driving and be capable of doing things that I can’t do. LINK2: Do you wear glasses? Or contact lenses? Then this is a familiar setting for you – and so is that feeling of disorientation when your vision is blurred. Now imagine you couldn’t correct that with a simple prescription. VO3: Instead, many visually impaired people rely on bulky assistive devices or help from friends and family to do basic daily tasks. But technology is opening up a whole new world. UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: eSight augments reality. So you’re able to magnify into your world. VO4: No, it’s not a Sci-fi movie. eSight is a wearable device that enhances the little vision Marlé has. A camera streams a live image to screens in front of her eyes, where she can manipulate it with a handheld control. UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: Control the contrast, control the colour, control the brightness in a way that their eyes might not be able to do for them. VO5: Now instead of pressing her nose to the blackboard, Marlé can digitally zoom in close enough to bypass her blind spot. She can freeze frame, change colours so text is easier to read, and stream video directly to her eyes. eSight can even read text aloud. UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: I looked out of the window and I saw on the water of the sea the little waves it made. The ocean just looks flat for me. And for the first time I could see that it’s wobbly and not flat. UPSOUND: Johan Grové: We have three grandchildren, little girls all of them. And it’s amazing for me because I can really see the detail on their faces, which wouldn’t be possible for me without this pair of glasses. VO6: Johan Grové was diagnosed with Stardgardt’s Disease at 15. As a Specific Needs consultant for Vodacom, he tests devices and programmes for accessibility. UPSOUND: Johan Grové: Having worked with assistive devices of all sorts and all sizes over 26 years, I have never come across a product like this that can do so many things in one device. I can even go on a game drive. There was giraffes about 100, 150m away on our right hand side. Normally I wouldn’t even bother looking because I just can’t see that far. And I could zoom in to a point where I could see the skin of the giraffe. VO7: Assistive tech was not what many of us had in mind when we were introduced to augmented reality. In fact, it was developed for completely different uses, from gaming to warfare. UPSOUND: Nicholas Rose: Being a military specification item, it’s robust and of course it’s real cool too. It projects a stereoscopic image of 65 inches like looking at a big TV set hovering in front of you. VO8: Sir Nicholas Rose discovered NuEyes after corneal ulcers demolished the vision in his left eye, and left his right cornea so scarred he sees as if through a misted window. Unable to recognise his patients, he was forced to end his 40-year career as an optometrist. UPSOUND: Nicholas Rose: I show-jumped international show-jumping, I played international polo on horseback, I did medieval armoured combat, I flew helicopters, I rode motorbikes, I did water skiing, yacht racing. Your life goes from 1000km/h to zero. VO9: NuEyes enhances a live image using this tiny remote, on-board controls, or voice commands. UPSOUND: Devi Sankaree Govender: Glasses make bigger. That’s like Harry Potter stuff! Well I can tell you even our camera crew look better with it on. Well done guys. Nicholas Rose: Now without the NuEyes I can’t even see this E. With the NuEyes I can get down to this 20/20 vision. Devi Sankaree Govender: I could do with a pair for spyware in my line of work. VO10: Nicholas has even begun work again as a low-vision optometrist distributing NuEyes. UPSOUND: Devi Sankaree Govender: How has this changed your life? Nicholas Rose: I can watch a polo game without holding up a pair of binoculars. I can watch polo. I can watch show jumping. And see it very clearly. I can go into a supermarket and see what we’re actually buying and what the prices are and that. UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: It’s sometimes the little things. So it allows them engagement in simple activities of daily living that some of us might take for granted. VO11: But few can afford the hefty dollar price tag. And these wearable devices only augment low vision: they’re useless to the totally blind. But another revolutionary assistive device is probably sitting in your pocket right now. LINK3: These days, we barely move without consulting an app. For most of us, a smart phone represents convenience, but for the visually impaired this little device is a lifeline. VO12: Many standard smart phones are now blind accessible and hundreds of apps offer assistance at an affordable price or even for free. They can identify colour, describe objects, recognise faces, and even narrate the world around you. UPSOUND: Johan Grové: In the past I had to run to the wine cooler, take out the bottle, come back to my wife, she’s busy preparing food. What is this, ok that’s not what I want, and you go back. So now it’s much easier. LINK4: Shopping for groceries – it’s such an everyday job. But try telling cinnamon from chilli when you can’t see the labels. UPSOUND: Johan Grové: That’s a Spier from the Spier landgoed. That’s good, we can take that one. VO13: Now Johan doesn’t have to see the label – he can use a QR and barcode scanner to identify the product he wants. UPSOUND: [app reads product name: House of Coffees] Johan Grové: House of Coffees Italian blend 250g. That’s exactly what I want. UPSOUND: Devi Sankaree Govender: What have the latest developments meant personally for you? Johan Grové: One word, independence. It gives you back your independence. It gives you the ability to take your phone, call a car, get in the car and drive somewhere. It gives me independence to read whatever I want to read wherever I am. UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: Machine learning is doing enormous progress in looking at the pictures and so on, but we still have a long way to go before you can really trust an algorithm to do this. VO14: Loss of his peripheral vision and years working with the blind inspired Hans Jørgen Wiberg to create Be My Eyes, a free app that connects a visually impaired person to a sighted volunteer via live video. UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: I like to call it micro-volunteering. We have quite a few calls that are like 20 seconds: Have I set my oven to 200 degrees? Yes you have. Oh, thank you very much. And so it’s a super super convenient way to be a volunteer. VO15: The app has 100 000 visually impaired users. 1.7 million volunteers have signed up to lend their eyes to the blind, who can now get 24/7 help from any time-zone, in 183 languages. UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: We even have had a blind girl who made a pregnancy test. And she was using Be My Eyes to have the result of this pregnancy test read to her. It’s really her only way to get this super personal information at her own terms. VO16: So while it remains to be seen what medical advances will do for the visually impaired, independence is cheaper and more available today than ever before. UPSOUND: Hans Jørgen Wiberg: Every time you have a friend over, then you have a long list of can you please do this and this and this. And now you can just drink coffee with your friends. UPSOUND: Marlé van Wyk: Ten years ago when I was diagnosed with the disease, there was nothing that could help me see better. It has given me opportunities that I’ve never had before. UPSOUND: Zoe Michaelides: If ever there was a time to be working with a preferred ability or different ability, it would be this time because people are able to compete on the same playing field in the digital world. PROMOS PROMO 1: 10 SECONDS VO: Over 250 million people worldwide live with impaired vision. It’s an age-old problem – but machine learning and augmented reality are offering new solutions. PROMO 2: 15 SECONDS VO: Assistive tech may not be the first thing that comes to mind when you hear the words “augmented reality”. But it’s opening up new worlds for the visually impaired. UPSOUND: [10:43:32][…] Nicholas: with the NuEyes I can get down to this 20/20 vision. Devi: I could do with a pair for spyware. PROMO 3: 15 SECONDS UPSOUND: [app reads product name: House of Coffees] Johan: House of Coffees Italian blend. That’s exactly what I want. VO: From high-end wearable devices to free apps, independence for the visually impaired is more available today than ever before. UPSOUND: Marle [10:14] […] it has given me opportunities that I’ve never had before. PROMO 4: 30 SECONDS UPSOUND: Marle [01:18] […] I can’t see my hand. It looks like my hand is cut off. But when it’s bringing it closer, it just looks like there is a hole in the middle of my hand. VO: Marle van Wyk is one of over 250 million people worldwide living with a visual impairment. But the age of augmented reality offers some cutting edge assistive solutions. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): How 21st century tech is assisting the blind and visually impaired
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Low tech solutions like white canes, guide dogs and Braille have been around for decades or even centuries to help make life a little easier for those who cannot see. But a new wave of smart technology, machine learning and virtual reality devices is changing the way the visually impaired are accessing the world around them.
metadata.Summary: Apps and smart devices have begun to dominate the way we interact with the world around us - and it's no different for people living with a visual impairment. From brand new (and pricey) wearable VR devices to smart refreshable braille (replacing 50s style braille typewriters) and even free apps, the world of assistive tech is expanding at a rapid pace - and perhaps even helping the blind to achieve a greater level of independence than ever before. We will look first at wearable devices, which have leveraged off the VR and MR technology released by Google and Microsoft in recent years. Although wearable VR did not take off as much as anticipated in the mainstream, it's had a big impact on assistive tech. We'll speak to two or three people who use different wearable devices about the impact they have had on their lives. We will also meet Mukthar Khan, who works for assistive tech company Sensory Solutions. He is blind himself and can talk about the challenges of being blind especially in SA, as well as the various devices developed to help. He will show us the refreshable braille device which allows import of text documents, note taking and interface with a phone - on one deceptively simple, small black box. He will also talk to us about the various apps that are available, often free of charge.
metadata.Further information: 1. WEARABLE DEVICES eSight is a wearable device that augments the vision of low-vision (or legally blind) people by filming the world in real time, projecting it onto screens in front of the user's eyes, and then magnifying and enhancing the images according to the user's needs. We'll speak to 17 year old Marle van Wyk, who says her life has been changed by eSight, and Johan Grove, who can show us how a user is assessed and fitted. NuEyes is another wearable device which was developed for use in the military. It operates in a very similar way to eSight but comes in at less than half the price, for $4500. 2. APPS Seeing AI is an app that uses image recognition and machine learning to recognise and describe faces, scenes and objects, and can read text on documents or street signs. It's developed by Microsoft and available for free. BeSpecular is a locally developed app that calls on crowd sourced volunteering. Both blind users and sighted volunteers download the app and sign up. Then when a blind person needs help with a task that requires sight (like picking a colour of shirt, reading a temperature gauge or a food label etc) they use the app to take a picture and record a voice message of their request. The request is sent to a number of sighted volunteers who can respond, listen to the message and type or record a response. This is a local version of other apps that are available around the world (another one is called Be My Eyes) and hopefully we will speak to the developer.
